bib.title: Telecommunications and Utilities (Chapter 10, The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 2nd ed.)

question: How do you review a draft dimensional schema for common design flaws, using a wireless-telecom billing case, and how should geographic location be modelled?
contributions: A design-review checklist of common dimensional modeling mistakes
A worked redesign of a draft customer-billing schema (Fig 10.2 to Fig 10.3)
Geographic location treated as a permissible snowflaked outrigger, with GIS integration

results.claim: A dimensional model typically has 5 to 15 dimensions; 2-3 or 25-30 signals a problem.
results.setup: Rule of thumb in design review checklist, no data
results.quote: a dimensional model typically has 5 to 15 dimensions
results.where: p.223, Too Many (or Too Few) Dimensions

limits: No empirical data; rules of thumb from the authors' consulting experience.
Does not cover handling of dimension attribute changes in this case (deferred: 'there's more ground to cover').
Billing case is a 2002 relational star-schema setting; call-detail grain was ruled out for feasibility, not modelled.
Location outrigger benefit is conditional: little gain if addresses barely overlap across dimensions; view-construct penalty depends on the DBMS.
practices: Ask for the fact table grain first and make team and business share one declaration of it (p.220, Granularity).
Build the fact table at the lowest grain available for the chosen business process, not the lowest data in the enterprise (p.220-221).

Keep all additive facts at the declared grain; drop year-to-date facts because they are not perfectly additive and invite double counting; compute YTD with a year constraint on the date dimension (p.221, p.225).
Give each dimension a single value per fact row and each attribute a single value per dimension row; collapse hierarchies into one dimension (p.221).
Avoid snowflaking dimensions; outriggers for low-cardinality or frequently reused attribute clusters are the exception (p.221).
Use a meaningful date dimension with roll-up and filter attributes; do not attach a generic date you cannot name the role of (p.222).
Replace fixed time-series buckets (month 1..12 columns) with separate fact rows per period (p.222).
Treat transaction numbers such as bill or invoice number as degenerate dimensions; a dimension with about as many rows as the fact table is the warning sign (p.222).
Put descriptive decodes next to every code as dimension data, not in the access application (p.222-223).
Use surrogate keys for all dimension primary keys and fact foreign keys; keep operational codes as attributes (p.223, p.225).
Move textual facts such as rate-plan type code into a dimension as roll-up attributes (p.224).

When a service line has a single customer, sales rep and rate plan but the service line dimension has millions of rows, model those as minidimensions of the service line rather than collapsing (p.224-225).
Model a shared location as an outrigger cloned per role via views with distinguishable column names, like date role-playing (p.226).
Add geospecific attributes (points, lines, polygons) to the location dimension, or geocode standardised addresses with a GIS tool, without changing existing applications (p.227).

terms.definition: Operational transaction numbers, such as the invoice or order number, kept in the fact table rather than given their own dimension.
A permissible snowflake: a dimension attached to another dimension, used for a cluster of low-cardinality or frequently reused attributes.
A separate dimension split out of a large, fast-growing dimension (here customer, sales rep, rate plan off the service line), per Chapter 6.
A phone number; each gets a bill line item and its own billing metrics.
A text value stored in the fact table; seldom sound, belongs in a dimension.
